explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Giving up is quiet, and this is the opposite. God says, "I am jealous for Zion with great zeal; I am jealous for her with great fervor." Great zeal AND great fervor. That is not someone heading for the door.

Right, friend. God says, "I am jealous for Zion with great zeal; I am jealous for her with great fervor." He says it twice, first with zeal and then with fervor. I think that's a God leaning in toward Zion, not walking away from her.
That's it, baker. God says, "I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem." The One returning is the LORD Himself. Then Jerusalem gets a brand new name, which is coming up.

explanations.answer: Scatter His people from it again
explanations.explanation: That one points the other way, friend. God says the opposite about His people. "I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem…" He says (Zechariah 8:8). So this is a gathering promise, not a scattering one.

explanations.answer: Hand it over to a new king
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but no king shows up in this verse. God says, "I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem." The one doing the returning is the LORD Himself. A new king would be a whole different story, and this passage doesn't tell it.

You got it, baker. God says, "…the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain." Jerusalem gets the name City of Truth, and the mountain gets its own name too. A city and a mountain, each with a new name.

Mount Carmel is a real mountain, friend. It's where Elijah, a prophet, told all Israel to meet him (1 Kings 18:19). But the name God gives in this passage is different. He says the mountain of the LORD of Hosts "…will be called the Holy Mountain."

The Mount of Olives is a real hill, baker, and the apostles returned to Jerusalem from it (Acts 1:12). It's just not the name God gives here. He says, "…the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain." Sometimes the answer is sitting right in the verse.

Yes, baker. God says, "Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem, each with a staff in hand because of great age." Notice the word "again." Sitting along the streets is the whole picture here.

Close, friend, but there's no wall-building here. God pictures old men and old women with a staff in hand because of great age. What He says they'll do is sit along the streets of Jerusalem. That's a picture of rest, not a work crew.

That's a fair guess, baker, but gates and guards aren't in this verse. God says the old men and old women will "…again sit along the streets of Jerusalem…" They each have a staff in hand because of great age. Sitting is the whole assignment, and I'd take that job.

That's the one, friend. God says, "…the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there." So the old folks sit on the streets, and the young ones play right alongside them. That's a lot of life in one city.

Marching sounds like soldiers, baker, and that's not the picture. God says the streets will be filled with boys and girls playing. The word is playing, and it fits right next to the old folks sitting down.

I see where that came from, friend. The question about weeping and fasting in the fifth month is what started all this (Zechariah 7:3). But in this verse, God says the streets will be filled with boys and girls playing. The weeping picture is getting swapped for a playing one.
Right, baker. God asks, "…should it also be impossible in My eyes?" The way He asks it, the answer is no. Right after that He keeps going with "I will save My people…" (Zechariah 8:7).

Not quite, friend. God doesn't say the remnant sees better. He sets two sets of eyes side by side: what looks impossible to them, and what He sees. Then He asks, "…should it also be impossible in My eyes?" His point is that what seems impossible to them is not impossible for Him.

explanations.answer: The promise may not come true
explanations.explanation: That's not where God is going, baker. He doesn't say "maybe." Right after His question, He says, "I will save My people from the land of the east and from the land of the west." (Zechariah 8:7). His question is leading to a promise, not a doubt.

True, friend. God says, "I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem, where they will be My people, and I will be their faithful and righteous God." Two promises are packed in there: the bringing back and the being their God. I wish every sentence of mine came with that much in it.

It's true, baker. God says, "I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem, where they will be My people, and I will be their faithful and righteous God." He says He'll bring them back, and He says who He'll be to them. Nothing in that verse is left hanging.

Yes, baker. God says, "Let your hands be strong, you who now hear these words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid to rebuild the temple…" He's talking to people who have work in front of them. And strong hands are exactly what any work needs, even stamping cookies.

explanations.answer: Let the work rest a while
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice break, friend, but God doesn't say it. He says, "Let your hands be strong…" That's a word for people who have work to do. It isn't a word for putting the tools down.

Priests aren't mentioned in this verse, baker. God speaks to people who now hear words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid. His message to them is, "Let your hands be strong…" He doesn't hand the job off to anyone else.

True, friend, and it's a heavy one. God says that before those days, "…neither man nor beast received wages, nor was there safety from the enemy for anyone who came or went, for I had turned every man against his neighbor." That's a hard picture of how things were. The next verse starts with "But now," and that's where the hope is.

It's actually true, baker, and it's a heavy verse. God says, "…for I had turned every man against his neighbor." That's how He describes the days before the temple rebuilding began. I think this is one to just let sit for a second, and then the "But now" comes.

That's it, friend. God says, "…the seed will be prosperous, the vine will yield its fruit, the ground will yield its produce, and the skies will give their dew." Then He says He'll give all of it to the remnant as an inheritance. It's a promise that the land will answer them.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will bring them gold
explanations.explanation: Gold is a fun guess, baker, but it's not in this verse. God talks about the seed, the vine, the ground and the dew. He says He'll give all these things to the remnant as an inheritance. The promise is about the land giving back.

That's a big promise, friend, but it's not the one God makes here. He says, "…the seed will be prosperous, the vine will yield its fruit, the ground will yield its produce, and the skies will give their dew." Walls don't come up. It's all about what grows.

Yes, baker. God says, "As you have been a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you will be a blessing." Same people, but a flip from curse to blessing. Then He adds, "Do not be afraid; let your hands be strong."
A warning sounds close, friend, but it's not the word. God says, "…so I will save you, and you will be a blessing." The word is blessing. That's the flip from curse that He promises.

I get why that came to mind, baker, because curse and burden feel like neighbors. But God says, "…so I will save you, and you will be a blessing." He saves them first, and then they become a blessing. It's the opposite of a burden.

Careful with this one, friend. God says He resolved to bring disaster when the fathers provoked Him to anger, "…and I did not relent…" The statement says He relented, and that's the part the text says didn't happen. It's a serious verse, and it sets up how big the change in verse 15 really is.

Right, baker. God says, "Just as I resolved to bring disaster upon you when your fathers provoked Me to anger, and I did not relent…" The part that doesn't fit is the relenting, because the text says He did not. It's a heavy verse, and the next one turns toward good.

explanations.answer: Do good again to Jerusalem and Judah
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God says, "so now I have resolved to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah." He resolved on disaster back then and didn't relent. Now He says He has resolved on good, and then adds, "Do not be afraid…"

explanations.answer: Wait and see how Judah behaves
explanations.explanation: That's a cautious answer, baker, but it's not what the verse says. God says, "so now I have resolved to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah." He says He has resolved, and no wait-and-see is in the verse.

explanations.answer: Bring disaster on all the nations
explanations.explanation: The verse goes a different direction, friend. God says He has resolved "…to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah." The disaster He mentions is what He resolved back then, when the fathers provoked Him to anger (Zechariah 8:14). Disaster on all the nations isn't what this verse says.

Yes, baker. God says, "These are the things you must do: Speak truth to one another, render true and sound judgments in your gates…" The list starts with plain honest talk between people. I like a list where the first item is something you can do before breakfast.

explanations.answer: Build a wall around the city
explanations.explanation: A wall is a solid idea, friend, but it's not on God's list. He says, "Speak truth to one another, render true and sound judgments in your gates…" The list is about how they treat each other. Nothing on it needs a ladder.

explanations.answer: Offer more sacrifices at the temple
explanations.explanation: Sacrifices don't show up on this list, baker. God says, "These are the things you must do: Speak truth to one another, render true and sound judgments in your gates…" The first thing He names is honest speech between neighbors.

That's the word, friend. God says, "…do not plot evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and do not love to swear falsely, for I hate all these things…" He doesn't say He tolerates them or shrugs. He says hate, and then He signs it, "declares the LORD…"

Allowing is a much softer word, baker, and it's not the one God uses. He says, "…do not plot evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and do not love to swear falsely, for I hate all these things…" The word is hate.

No rewards here, friend. God says, "…do not plot evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and do not love to swear falsely, for I hate all these things…" The verse puts plotting evil and swearing falsely together as things He hates, so nothing about a payoff.

You got it, baker. God says the fasts of the fourth, the fifth, the seventh and the tenth months "…will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." Those four fasts get a whole new meaning. And this is how the passage answers the fasting question from the beginning (Zechariah 7:3).
Other way around, friend. God says those fasts "…will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." Mourning goes out, joy comes in.

That's not in the verse, baker. God says the fasts of the fourth, the fifth, the seventh and the tenth months will become times of joy and gladness. He calls them "…cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." No fasting for a select few is mentioned.

That's it, friend. God says, "Therefore you are to love both truth and peace." It comes right after the promise that the fasts become cheerful feasts. So the joy comes, and He tells them what to love.

That's a fun guess, baker, but the feasts are the gift, not the thing to love. God says the fasts will become cheerful feasts, and then, "Therefore you are to love both truth and peace." Songs aren't in the verse.

Land and harvest were in the earlier promises, friend, but not here. In this verse, after the fasts become cheerful feasts, God says, "Therefore you are to love both truth and peace." That's the pair He names.

explanations.answer: Let us go and seek the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The residents of one city will go to another, saying, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." They don't say it to themselves. They say it to the people in the other city.

explanations.answer: Let us go and trade in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Trading is a reasonable reason to travel, friend, but it's not what they say. They say, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." The trip is about the LORD, not business.

explanations.answer: Let us go and see the new walls
explanations.explanation: Sightseeing sounds nice, baker, but no walls are in this verse. The residents of one city say to another, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." They're headed there to seek the LORD.

True, friend. The ones doing the inviting say, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." Then they add, "I myself am going." That's not a "you go ahead, I'll catch up later." They're in.
It's actually true, baker. The ones doing the inviting say, "I myself am going." They're not sending someone else down the road. They're going too.

Not quite, friend. God doesn't say a few small nations. He says, "…many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Hosts in Jerusalem and to plead before the LORD." Many and strong, not few and small.

Right, baker. God says, "…many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Hosts in Jerusalem and to plead before the LORD." He says many peoples, and He says strong nations. That's a big crowd, and it's nothing like a few small nations.

explanations.answer: We have heard that God is with you
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. These men say, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you." Their reason is what they've heard about God being with them. It's a lovely way to end the chapter, and I mean that.

explanations.answer: We have lost our way in the city
explanations.explanation: Getting lost would be a fair reason to grab a stranger's robe, baker, but it's not theirs. They say, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you." They're not looking for directions.

explanations.answer: We have come to collect a debt
explanations.explanation: That grip sounds like a bill collector, friend, but that's not what these men say. They say, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you." They're holding on because of what they've heard about God.
